Now let me compile all the research into verse-by-verse notes.

---

# 2 Kings 17:1–20 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Passage

This chapter records the fall of the Northern Kingdom of Israel to Assyria (c. 722 BC) and then gives an extended theological explanation of *why* it happened. Matthew Henry notes that the chapter "gives us an account of the captivity of the ten tribes, and so finishes the history of that kingdom, after it had continued about 265 years, from the setting up of Jeroboam the son of Nebat."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/17.htm

The Pulpit Commentary notes that vv. 7–23 form "an independent section by itself" where the writer "ceases to be the mere historian, and becomes the religious teacher and prophet, drawing out the lessons of history, and justifying the ways of God to man."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

Dale Ralph Davis (cited at Precept Austin) divides vv. 7–23 into three parts marked by the Hebrew word *kāʿas* ("provoke"): vv. 7–12, 13–17, and 18–23 — each beginning with a distinct theological affirmation: Yahweh brought Israel from Egypt (v. 7), Yahweh warned Israel by prophets (v. 13), and Yahweh was angry enough to banish them (v. 18).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary

---

## v. 1: "In the twelfth year of the reign of Ahaz over Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria nine years."

**Traditional reading:** Hoshea, whose name means "salvation" or "deliverance," assassinated Pekah to take the throne (2 Kings 15:30). His reign began c. 732 BC and ended in 722 BC with the fall of Samaria. He was the last king of the Northern Kingdom — the 19th king after Solomon. The chronological note ("twelfth year of Ahaz") appears to conflict with 2 Kings 15:30, which places Hoshea's conspiracy "in the twentieth year of Jotham." Various solutions are proposed: some suggest a co-regency of Jotham and Ahaz, or that Hoshea was not fully recognized as king until the twelfth year of Ahaz after an interregnum.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Historical note:** Paul House observes that "a long time has passed since the prophet Ahijah told the wife of Jeroboam I that idolatry would lead to Israel's exile (1 Kgs 14:14–16). Over these two hundred years Israel has seemed determined to make this prophecy come to pass. No reform occurs. No real repentance emerges."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary

---

## v. 2: "And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, but not like the kings of Israel who preceded him."

**Traditional reading:** Hoshea was evil, but "not as" his predecessors — a restrained evaluation. The Pulpit Commentary says he "maintained the calf-worship" but "was not guilty of any special wickedness — he set up no new idolatry" and apparently allowed subjects to attend festival worship at Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:11, 18). Jewish tradition adds that when the golden calf of Bethel had been carried off by the Assyrians, he did not replace it.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** "Hoshea was an evil man, but by no means the worst of the kings of Israel. Sadly, his bloody overthrow of the preceding king and violent ascent to power did not make him unusually evil among the kings of Israel." Guzik notes this illustrates that "judgment may not come at the height of sin" — God has the big picture in view. He quotes Trapp: "It is not the last sand that exhausteth the hour-glass, nor the last stroke of the axe that felleth the tree; so here."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

**Precept Austin:** "Partial restraint from evil is not the same as obedience. Moderation in sin does not substitute for faithfulness to the LORD… Partial disobedience is not a lesser form of obedience but a complete failure to obey."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill notes Hoshea did not worship Baal as some predecessors had, and could not worship the calves because they had been carried away in prior Assyrian incursions. Jewish tradition says he removed the border garrisons that prevented Israelites from going to Jerusalem; this was later commemorated as a festival.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

---

## v. 3: "Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked him, and Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute."

**Traditional reading:** Shalmaneser V (727–722 BC) succeeded his father Tiglath-Pileser III. Hoshea, who had been placed on the throne as an Assyrian vassal by Tiglath-Pileser, apparently revolted upon the father's death. Shalmaneser marched against him, and Hoshea submitted, becoming a tribute-paying vassal.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary

**Precept Austin:** Notes the irony — "Hoshea who refused to serve the LORD would now be forced to serve a pagan empire." The Hebrew word for tribute (*minchah*) is also the standard word for a grain offering, highlighting the humiliation: what should have been offered to God was now extorted by a pagan king.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary

---

## v. 4: "But the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea had conspired to send envoys to King So of Egypt, and that he had not paid tribute to the king of Assyria as in previous years. Therefore the king of Assyria arrested Hoshea and put him in prison."

**Traditional reading:** Hoshea sought an alliance with Egypt against Assyria, a strategy repeatedly condemned by the prophet Hosea (Hosea 7:11; 12:1). When he withheld tribute, Shalmaneser discovered the conspiracy, imprisoned Hoshea, and invaded Israel.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Who was "So, king of Egypt"?** The Pulpit Commentary identifies "So" (Hebrew סוֹא) as the Ethiopian pharaoh Shabak (Shebek), known to the Assyrians as Sibakhi. Patterson and Austel (cited by Guzik) suggest "So" is better understood as the city "Sais," then the capital of Egypt: "he had sent envoys to Sais (even unto) the king of Egypt."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** "As we might expect among the kings of Israel, Hoshea did not look to the LORD for help — he looked to Egypt. Therefore, Hosea said of him: *As for Samaria, her king is cut off like a twig on the water* (Hosea 10:7)."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill notes that the Assyrian king "had intelligence by spies he sent" and that Hoshea was arrested — though Gill thinks this probably occurred after the siege of Samaria rather than before.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

---

## v. 5: "Then the king of Assyria invaded the whole land, marched up to Samaria, and besieged it for three years."

**Traditional reading:** The Assyrian army spread throughout the land and laid siege to Samaria. The siege lasted about three years (from Hoshea's 7th year to his 9th). The Pulpit Commentary notes that by Hebrew reckoning of inclusive years, the actual duration may have been shorter — perhaps just over a year — though it could have stretched nearly three full years.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Historical note:** Samaria's walls, built by Omri and Ahab, were formidable. Dilday (cited by Guzik) says: "The fact that it took Assyria that long to break Samaria's resistance is a testimony to the good wall Omri and Ahab had built around the capital city."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

**Ellicott:** Notes that Shalmaneser probably besieged the city for about two years before his death; Sargon II then finished the siege. "Sargon states that he took Samaria (Samerína) in his first year."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/17.htm (from search excerpt)

---

## v. 6: "In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried away the Israelites to Assyria, where he settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes."

**Traditional reading:** Samaria fell in 722 BC. The Assyrians deported most of the population and resettled them in various locations across the Assyrian Empire. The Pulpit Commentary identifies Halah with the Chalcitis of Ptolemy (near the Khabour River), Habor as the Western Khabour river (a tributary of the Euphrates), and Gozan as Gauzanitis/Mygdonia. The "cities of the Medes" shows that Media was then under Assyrian control.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Guzik (Enduring Word):** Describes the humiliation of Assyrian deportation: captives were "led away on journeys of hundreds of miles… naked and attached together with a system of strings and fishhooks pierced through their lower lips," fulfilling Amos 4:2–3. He notes Sargon II's own inscription claims credit for the capture: "I clashed with them and took as booty 27,280 people with their chariots and their gods in whom they trusted."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

**On the "Lost Tribes":** Guzik argues the northern tribes were never truly "lost." When Jeroboam I instituted calf-worship, the faithful priests, Levites, and other godly Israelites migrated south to Judah (2 Chronicles 11:13–16), so "the Southern Kingdom of Judah contained Israelites from all of the ten tribes." Others assimilated, and some kept their identity in exile.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

---

## v. 7: "All this happened because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt. They had worshiped other gods…"

**Traditional reading:** This verse introduces the theological cause of the catastrophe. The downfall was not geopolitical but spiritual. The Pulpit Commentary says the clauses from v. 7 to v. 17 all depend on "when"; the apodosis does not come until v. 18. The mention of the Exodus highlights Israel's ingratitude and makes their sin especially heinous — the God who redeemed them is the one they abandoned.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Reformed (Ligonier):** "The ultimate cause of Israel's expulsion from the land was flagrant covenant violation, especially the grievous sin of idolatry. Thinking they could rebel against the Lord with impunity, God's covenant people brought judgment on their own heads, just as their covenant Lord promised would happen (Lev. 26:14–39)." The immediate political trigger (rebellion against Assyria) was only the surface cause; God's perspective is what matters.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/consequences-sin (from search excerpt)

**Matthew Henry:** Notes that the sacred historian overlooks "second causes — the weakness of Israel, their impolitic management, and the strength and growing greatness of the Assyrian monarch" — and looks only to the First Cause. "It was the Lord that removed Israel out of his sight; whoever were the instruments, he was the author of this calamity."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/17.htm

**Baptist (Gill):** Emphasizes the ingratitude: God "had brought them up out of the land of Egypt, from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt; which is observed to show their ingratitude, and to aggravate their sin of idolatry."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

---

## v. 8: "and walked in the customs of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites, as well as in the practices introduced by the kings of Israel."

**Traditional reading:** Israel's guilt was twofold: (1) they adopted Canaanite idolatrous customs, and (2) they followed the state-sponsored innovations of their own kings — primarily Jeroboam's calf-worship. The Pulpit Commentary distinguishes the two sources: "the great majority were derived from the heathen nations… adopted voluntarily by the people themselves. A certain number, however, came in… imposed upon the people by their kings."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Ellicott:** "The national guilt was twofold. It comprised: (1) idolatry in the strict sense — i.e., worship of other gods than Jehovah; (2) a heathenish mode of worshipping Jehovah Himself — namely, under the form of a bullock, as Jeroboam I. had ordained."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/17.htm (from search excerpt)

**Guzik (Enduring Word):** "God cast out the Canaanite nations in the days of Joshua because of these sins. Now He had cast out the Northern Kingdom of Israel for the same sins. God's judgment was not against the ancient Canaanites because of race or ethnicity; it was because of their conduct. As Israel shared the same conduct, they would share the same judgment."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

---

## v. 9: "The Israelites secretly did things against the LORD their God that were not right. From watchtower to fortified city, they built high places in all their cities."

**Traditional reading:** The Hebrew word translated "secretly" (יחפאו) may mean they "covered" or disguised their actions with plausible pretexts — though some dispute this rendering and say it means they made their deeds a barrier between themselves and God. "From watchtower to fortified city" is a proverbial expression meaning everywhere, from the smallest solitary outpost to the largest walled city. The "high places" were unauthorized places of sacrifice, contrary to the command to worship only at the Jerusalem temple.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Baptist (Gill):** Notes the people were "partly conscious to themselves that they were not right, and ashamed to commit them openly; and partly as foolishly imagining, that, being done privately, they were not seen and observed of God."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Guzik (Enduring Word):** "Rebellion and sin cloud the judgment of men, and clearly the judgment of Israel was affected. Their judgment was impaired enough to think they could sin secretly against the God who sees everything."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

---

## v. 10: "They set up for themselves sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree."

**Traditional reading:** "Sacred pillars" (*matsevoth*) were stone pillars anciently connected with Baal worship. "Asherah poles" (or "groves" in the KJV) were wooden cult objects associated with the Canaanite goddess Asherah. The locations — "every high hill" and "every green tree" — were typical Canaanite worship sites. The Pulpit Commentary notes that since these "groves" were "set up under green trees," they must have been artificial structures, not living trees.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Baptist (Gill):** Illustrates by comparison: "so the Indians to this day have idols dispersed here and there in the fields, placed in little groves, or at the foot of some hill that casts a shadow."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

---

## v. 11: "They burned incense on all the high places like the nations that the LORD had driven out before them. They did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger."

**Traditional reading:** Incense symbolized prayer (Psalm 141:2) and should have been offered only on the golden altar in the temple. By burning incense at the high places, Israel imitated the very nations God had expelled from Canaan. The Pulpit Commentary notes: "The offering of incense to their gods by the Canaanitish nations had not been previously mentioned; but the use of incense in religious worship was so widely spread in the ancient world, that their employment of it might have been assumed as almost certain."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

The phrase "provoking the LORD to anger" (Hebrew *kāʿas*) is one of the structural markers of the passage (Dale Ralph Davis).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary

---

## v. 12: "They served idols, although the LORD had told them, 'You shall not do this thing.'"

**Traditional reading:** The Hebrew word for idols here is *gillulim* — a rare, contemptuous term used frequently by Ezekiel. Its root *galal* means "dung," so it carries a derogatory force: "dung-gods." The explicit command broken here is Exodus 20:4–5.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Baptist (Gill):** "Dunghill gods, as the word signifies… and Sterculius was one of the names of Saturn, an Heathen deity, which he had, as is supposed, by his finding out the method of making land fruitful with dung."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

---

## v. 13: "Yet through all His prophets and seers, the LORD warned Israel and Judah, saying, 'Turn from your wicked ways and keep My commandments and statutes, according to the entire Law that I commanded your fathers and delivered to you through My servants the prophets.'"

**Traditional reading:** God did not bring judgment without abundant warning. The prophets and seers (terms used synonymously, 1 Samuel 9:9) were sent continually to both kingdoms. The Pulpit Commentary lists the succession: in Israel — Ahijah, Jehu son of Hanani, Elijah, Micaiah, Elisha, Jonah, Hosea, Amos, Oded; in Judah — Shemaiah, Iddo, Azariah, Hanani, Jehu, Jahaziel, Eliezer, Zechariah, Joel, Micah, Isaiah, and others. Their consistent message was: "Turn from your evil ways."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** "In love, God sent prophets to the Northern and Southern Kingdoms. Their message was a warning against the sins that corrupted God's people and separated them from their God." Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "Their sin was first against law, but finally it was against patient love."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasizes covenant theology: God "testified against" them as a prosecuting witness, and the prophets functioned as "covenant lawsuit" messengers.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/consequences-sin (from search excerpt)

---

## v. 14: "But they would not listen, and they stiffened their necks like their fathers, who did not believe the LORD their God."

**Traditional reading:** "Stiffened their necks" is a metaphor from stubborn oxen that refuse to bow to the yoke. Matthew Poole (cited by Guzik) says: "Refused to submit their neck to the yoke of God's precepts; a metaphor from stubborn oxen, that make their necks hard, or stiff, and will not bow to the yoke." The comparison to "their fathers" refers especially to the wilderness generation who did not believe God and were therefore barred from Canaan (Numbers 14; Deuteronomy 9:6, 13).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Guzik:** "God sent these messengers to help Israel and to spare them the judgment that would come if they did not turn from their evil ways. Yet God's people became more stubborn when God brought this call to repentance, and they sank deeper into sin."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

---

## v. 15: "They rejected His statutes and the covenant He had made with their fathers, as well as the decrees He had given them. They pursued worthless idols and themselves became worthless, going after the surrounding nations that the LORD had commanded them not to imitate."

**Traditional reading:** This is one of the most theologically significant verses in the chapter. The Pulpit Commentary states: "False gods are 'vanity'; false religions are 'vanity'; there is nothing firm or substantial about them… And the followers of such religions derive weakness from them — they 'become vain' — i.e., weak, futile, impotent."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**On the Hebrew word *hebel*:** Dilday (cited by Guzik) explains: "The original is more accurate at this point: 'They worshipped emptiness and became empty.' The word here is *hebel* meaning 'air,' 'delusion,' or 'vanity.' The idea is that they became like the gods they worshipped. They bowed down to nothingness and became nothing."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

**Baptist (Gill):** "They followed vanity; idols, which are vain things for help, can neither hear, see, speak, etc. and became vain as sottish and stupid as the idols they worshipped; which is the usual fruit and effect of idolatry, see Romans 1:21."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Precept Austin / D.A. Carson:** "'They followed worthless idols and themselves became worthless' (2 Kings 17:15; cf. Jer. 2:5)." Carson notes this is a key spiritual principle: we become like what we worship.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary

---

## v. 16: "They abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God and made for themselves two cast idols of calves and an Asherah pole. They bowed down to all the host of heaven and served Baal."

**Traditional reading:** This verse summarizes the national apostasy. The "two cast idols of calves" refers to Jeroboam I's state-sponsored cult at Dan and Bethel (1 Kings 12:26–29). The Pulpit Commentary notes that while the calf-worship was imposed by Jeroboam, Baal and Asherah worship was introduced by Ahab (1 Kings 16:31–33). Worship of "the host of heaven" (sun, moon, stars) came later and is specifically associated with Manasseh in Judah (2 Kings 21:3).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Baptist (Gill):** Notes that Baal worship "was service to the sun, as Abarbinel interprets it; this was the god of the Zidonians Ahab worshipped, having married a princess of that people" (1 Kings 16:31). He also cites James 2:10: "he that offends in one point is guilty of them all."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Ellicott:** Notes that "molten images" is literally "a casting" (singular), referring to the single mold used for both calves.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/17.htm (from search excerpt)

---

## v. 17: "They sacrificed their sons and daughters in the fire and practiced divination and soothsaying. They devoted themselves to doing evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger."

**Traditional reading:** Child sacrifice refers to the cult of Molech (Moloch), to whom children were burned. "Divination and soothsaying" were expressly forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10. "Sold themselves" (in some translations) means they willingly became slaves to sin — the Pulpit Commentary notes the allusion to Ahab who "sold himself to do evil" (1 Kings 21:20).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Baptist (Gill):** On child sacrifice: "This was done either by way of lustration, or so as to be burnt." On divination: they sought "knowledge of what was to be done at present, or of things to come, neglecting the word of God and his prophets." On "sold themselves": "they were as much the servants of sin as if they had sold themselves to be slaves to it."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Ellicott:** "Idolatry is regarded as a servitude."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/17.htm (from search excerpt)

---

## v. 18: "So the LORD was very angry with Israel, and He removed them from His presence. Only the tribe of Judah remained…"

**Traditional reading:** This is the apodosis — the conclusion of the long indictment begun in v. 7. "Removed them from His presence" means banishment from the land of promise, where God had dwelt among His people. It does not mean they escaped His omniscient sight; rather, they lost all tokens of His favor. "Only the tribe of Judah remained" — though Benjamin, Simeon, and many individuals from the northern tribes who had migrated south were also included.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Baptist (Gill):** "Removed them out of his sight; not out of the reach of his all seeing eye, but from all tokens of his favour, from the good land he had given them, and all the benefits and privileges of it."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Notes that while believers in Christ "need not fear that we will be exiled from the blessed presence of God forever," God may still discipline us for sin, "and we may feel the effects of His disciplinary rod on the covenant community just as the righteous remnant went into exile along with the unfaithful Israelites."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/consequences-sin (from search excerpt)

---

## v. 19: "and even Judah did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but lived according to the customs Israel had introduced."

**Traditional reading:** Judah was more faithful than Israel, yet not innocent. The Pulpit Commentary sees this as a parenthesis — a warning that Judah also imitated the sins of the northern kingdom and would share a similar fate. The "statutes of Israel" refer particularly to the corrupt religious practices introduced by Israel's kings, which infected Judah especially under Ahaziah (2 Kings 8:27) and Ahaz (2 Kings 16:3).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Baptist (Gill):** "Also Judah kept not the commandments of the Lord their God, but were infected with the idolatry of the ten tribes, and drawn into it by their example, and persisted therein, notwithstanding what befell the ten tribes; which are aggravations of the sins of them both, see Jeremiah 3:7."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Guzik (Enduring Word):** "Judah had the lesson right in front of them — the conquered nation of Israel was evidence of what happened when hearts turned from God. Yet they ignored these plain lessons and imitated the sins of Israel."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

---

## v. 20: "So the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel. He afflicted them and delivered them into the hands of plunderers, until He had banished them from His presence."

**Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary says "all the seed of Israel" here means the entire nation — Israel in the widest sense, both kingdoms. "Rejected" (*māʾas*) differs from "cast out" (*hišlîk mippānāyw*): the former refers to chastening judgments (famine, drought, pestilence — Amos 4:6) aimed at bringing repentance; the latter is the final exile. The "spoilers" include the Syrians under Hazael and Ben-Hadad (2 Kings 10:32; 13:3), the Assyrians under Tiglath-Pileser (2 Kings 15:19, 29), and later the Babylonians against Judah.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html

**Ellicott:** Notes the LXX reads differently: "And they rejected the Lord, and the Lord was angry with all the seed of Israel." Thenius prefers this reading, making the writer go back to v. 18 after the parenthesis about Judah.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/17.htm (from search excerpt); also https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/17-20.htm

**Baptist (Gill):** "The Lord rejected all the seed of Israel… with loathing and contempt, and wrote a 'loammi' on them, rejected them from being his people, gave them a bill of divorce, and declared them no more under his care and patronage." Gill lists afflictions before the final casting off: "famine, drought, and pestilence, Amos 4:6."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Matthew Henry:** "God is no respecter of persons. As he had rejected the ten tribes on account of certain transgressions… so, when Judah committed the self-same sins, and transgressed equally, Judah had equally to be rejected."
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/17-20.htm

---

## Summary of Distinctive Protestant Perspectives

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasizes God's sovereignty in judgment, the covenant lawsuit pattern, and the ultimate cause as covenant violation rather than political miscalculation. Points forward to Christ: only in Him is there deliverance from the exile of sin.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/consequences-sin (from search excerpt)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasizes the practical spiritual principle that "we become like what we worship" (from *hebel* in v. 15). Applies the text to modern believers: "When we give our hearts to false gods or split our loyalty between God and the world, we become like the empty things we worship, and God's patient warnings eventually give way to His judgment." Warns against "mongrel faith" (from vv. 24–41).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/

**Baptist (Gill):** A strong emphasis on the specific Old Testament laws broken (citing Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy chapter and verse for each sin) and on the just nature of the punishment. Gill uniquely connects the Hebrew word for idols (*gillulim*, "dung-gods") to the Roman god Sterculius. He also brings in Jewish rabbinic traditions (Seder Olam, Talmud).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html

**Methodist/Wesleyan:** No distinct Wesleyan commentary on this passage was located among the specified sites. Matthew Henry (non-conformist, but widely used across traditions) emphasizes God's justice and patience, and the people's own responsibility: "by their way and their doings they procured all this to themselves, and it was their own wickedness that did correct them."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/17.htm

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (Historical):** Multiple sources note the discrepancy between the biblical account (which names Shalmaneser V as the besieger) and Assyrian records (where Sargon II claims the capture). The resolution generally held is that Shalmaneser began the siege and Sargon completed it after Shalmaneser's death in 722 BC. Sargon's prism inscription claims he took 27,280 captives from Samaria. The Eponym Canon confirms Shalmaneser reigned 727–722 BC and was succeeded by Sargon II.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary
